title: Explaining a Discount
subtitle: How to explain a price reduction clearly and confidently in English
description: A good salesperson does not just give a lower price — they explain it well. This lesson teaches simple, clear language for talking about discounts: how to say how much something costs after a reduction, how much the customer saves, and how long the offer is available.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley explains a special discount to Marcus — and helps him understand exactly what he saves

vocabulary.definition: A reduction in the price of something. When you give a discount, you charge less than the normal price.
vocabulary.example: Marcus said the price was too high, so Riley offered a discount. She said: We can give you a 20% discount — that saves you $100 every month.

vocabulary.definition: One part in every hundred. We use percent to show how big a discount is. The symbol is %.
vocabulary.example: Riley told Marcus: The plan is 20 percent off this month. That means you pay 20% less than the original price.

vocabulary.definition: To keep money by paying less than normal. When there is a discount, the customer saves money.
vocabulary.example: Riley explained the value clearly: You save $100 every month with this plan. That is $1,200 every year.

vocabulary.definition: A good offer where you pay less money than usual. A deal is something the customer benefits from.
vocabulary.example: Riley introduced the promotion with confidence: We are running a special deal this month — the best price we have offered all year.

vocabulary.definition: The first or normal price, before any discount or change.
vocabulary.example: Riley made the saving clear by comparing prices: The original price is $500 per month. With the discount, you only pay $400.

vocabulary.definition: Not available for a long time. A limited offer has an end date — the customer cannot wait forever.
vocabulary.example: Riley created urgency without pressure: This is a limited offer. We can only hold this price until the end of the month.

vocabulary.definition: A special price or opportunity available for a short period of time.
vocabulary.example: The sales manager approved a special offer for new customers: Sign up before Friday and get the first month free.

vocabulary.definition: Still active and usable. A discount or offer is valid until a certain date — after that date, it is gone.
vocabulary.example: Marcus asked how long the price would last. Riley said: This price is valid until the 31st. After that, it goes back to normal.

phrasalVerbs.definition: The standard way to state a discount. 'Off' means the price is lower than normal. You can replace 20% with any number.
phrasalVerbs.example: A customer asked about the price. Riley said: Good news — it is 20% off this month. That is the lowest price we have had all year.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Tell the customer exactly how much money they save. This makes the discount feel real and personal — not just a number.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus was not sure if the discount was big enough. Riley said: You save $100 every month — that is $1,200 a year. That is real money.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Use this to show the comparison between the normal price and the discounted price. It helps the customer see the value.
phrasalVerbs.example: Riley wanted Marcus to see the saving clearly: The original price is $500 per month. With your discount, you pay $400. That is a real reduction.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Tell the customer the offer will not last. It creates urgency — but say it calmly, not as pressure.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus said he needed more time. Riley responded: Of course, take your time — but I want you to know this is a limited offer. It ends on Friday.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: We are running a special deal
phrasalVerbs.definition: A natural way to introduce a discount in conversation. Use it at the start to get the customer interested.
phrasalVerbs.example: The customer did not know about any promotion. Riley said: Actually, we are running a special deal this month — let me tell you about it.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Use this to give the customer a clear deadline. Always follow it with a specific date so they know exactly when the offer ends.
phrasalVerbs.example: Marcus asked how long he had to decide. Riley said: This price is valid until the 30th of this month — so you have about two weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Riley, I really like the Standard Plan. But the price is a little high for us right now.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I understand, Marcus. Actually, we are running a special [[deal:a good offer where you pay less money than usual]] this month.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: The Standard Plan is 20% off right now. That is a good [[discount:a reduction in the price of something]] for you.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Okay. What is the original price?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: The [[original:the first or normal price, before any discount]] price is $500 per month. With the discount, you pay $400.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: So how much do I save?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: You [[save:to keep money by paying less than normal]] $100 every month. That is $1,200 every year.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: That is a lot of money. Is this a limited offer?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Yes, this is a [[limited:not available for a long time]] offer. This price is [[valid:still active and usable]] until the end of the month.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I need to talk to my manager first. Can you send me the details?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Of course. I will send you an email with all the information today.

completeSentenceExercise.instructions: Choose the correct word to complete each sentence. Only one answer is correct.

items.sentence: The Standard Plan is 20% _____ this month.
items.explanation: We say '20% off' to show a price reduction. 'Off' means the price is lower than normal. 'On' and 'from' are not used this way.

items.sentence: You _____ $100 every month with this discount.
items.explanation: 'Save' means you keep money because the price is lower. 'Spend' and 'pay' mean you give money — the opposite of what we mean here.

items.sentence: The _____ price is $500. With the discount, you pay $400.
items.explanation: 'Original' means the normal price before the discount. 'New' suggests a recent change. 'Final' usually means there are no more changes.

items.sentence: This is a _____ offer — it ends on Friday.
items.explanation: 'Limited' is the standard word for an offer that has an end date. 'Short' describes time, not an offer. 'Small' describes size.

items.sentence: We are running a special _____ this month.
items.explanation: 'Deal' is the natural word here — 'running a special deal' is a common sales phrase. 'Price' and 'percent' do not fit this sentence pattern.

items.sentence: This price is _____ until the end of the month.
items.explanation: 'Valid' means the price is still active and usable until that date. 'Ready' and 'open' are not used this way for prices or offers.

chooseResponse.instructions: Read what the customer says. Choose the best response from the three options.

items.customerLine: Is there any discount available right now?
options: Yes, the plan is 20% off this month — it is our best current offer.
The original price is $500 per month.
I can send you an email with the details.
items.explanation: Option A answers the question directly and clearly states the discount. Option B gives a price but does not answer whether there is a discount. Option C avoids the question completely.

items.customerLine: How much money do I save with this discount?
options: This is a limited offer, so you should decide soon.
You save $100 every month — that is $1,200 every year.
items.explanation: Option C gives the customer a specific, personal answer — the exact amount saved. Option A talks about urgency but does not answer the question. Option B repeats the percentage, which the customer may already know.

items.customerLine: When does this special price end?
options: We are running a special deal this month.
This price is valid until the end of the month.
The original price is $500 per month.
items.explanation: Option B answers the question with a clear deadline. Option A introduces the deal but does not say when it ends. Option C is about the original price, not the deadline.

spotTheMistake.instructions: Read the conversation. Three lines have a mistake. Can you find them?

dialogue.text: We have a great deal this month on the Business Plan.

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Really? How much is the discount?

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.text: Good. And how much do I save?

mistakes.explanation: We say '20% off', not '20% on'. 'Off' shows the price is lower. 'On' does not have this meaning in English.
A discount means you keep more money, so you 'save' — not 'spend'. 'Spend' means you give money. 'Save' means you keep it.
We say 'valid until' a date, not 'valid from'. 'Until' tells the customer when the offer ends. 'From' suggests when it starts.
